new_statements.quote: [p.3] Assumption 2 Old Nubian metrical feet are trochees, the rightmost foot being the heaviest: (σ́.σ). Note that it is unclear whether prosodic heaviness was expressed through a tonal or a stress accent. Assumption 3 Metrical feet are assigned from left to right. Assumption 4 The main stress on a root is fixed. [...] [p.6] Just like a few other forms we encountered above, these show that although Old Nubian feet are trochees, roots can have main stress either on the first or the second syllable. This is lexically determined. [...] [p.7] Lemma 2 Bisyllabic roots can have stress either on the first (default) or on the second syllable (marked). The second syllable may be either full (ⲕⲁⲡⲟⲡ) or defective (ⲥⲟⲩⲕⲕ).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Reconstructed (dead language, no accent marking in the script): prosodic words are parsed into trochaic feet from the left edge; the root carries a fixed main stress, on its first syllable by default, on its second syllable in a lexically marked class (identified from non-assimilation/epenthesis behaviour and, for Greek loans, from the Greek accent, which is assumed to be preserved). Most suffixes are unstressed, but imperative subject clitics (-e, -ana) attract stress (p.8). Whether the prominence was stress or a tonal accent is left open.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Transcriptions mark a secondary prominence on later trochaic feet (e.g. /ma.ti"ti.si-gu.gil.le/, /"dek.ki-giR.mis-se.lo/), implied by left-to-right trochaic footing with 'the rightmost foot being the heaviest'; no explicit secondary-stress rule is formulated.
new_statements.exceptions: Lexically marked roots with second-syllable stress (e.g. kapop-, doutrap-, soukk-, tans-, au-, pann-); 'defective' roots ending in an incomplete stressed syllable; Greek loanwords keep Greek stress (Assumption 5); imperative 2/3 subject clitics -e/-ana attract stress; 'labile roots' in final -r/-l show edge alternations irrespective of stress (sec.3.7).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the prosodic word (root plus suffix/clitic chain; p.5 notes one prosodic word can contain two lexical words). Entirely inferred from manuscript spellings (assimilation, deletion, epenthesis) and comparison with Kenzi/Nobiin; author states ON writing had no means of expressing stress or tone (p.1) and that stress vs tonal accent is undecidable (p.3).
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Old Nubian proper (oldn1245 / ISO onw), the literary language of the medieval Nubian kingdoms; no dialect split. Note: every statement about ON stress is a RECONSTRUCTION from spelling (assimilation/epenthesis patterns and Greek loanword accent), not an observed prosody; the author explicitly says it is unclear whether the prominence was a stress or a tonal accent. Modern Nile Nubian relatives (Nobiin nobi1240, Kenzi kenu1236, Dongolawi dong1288) are separate glottocodes with their own descriptions.

sources.locator: p.3 (Assumptions 2-4), p.6 (end of sec.3.4) and p.7 (Lemma 2); also p.1 and p.8
sources.note: Reconstructs ON prosody from assimilation/epenthesis/deletion patterns and Greek loan accent: feet are trochees assigned left-to-right, rightmost foot heaviest; main stress fixed on the root; bisyllabic roots stressed on 1st syllable (default) or 2nd (lexically marked); imperative subject clitics attract stress; assimilation restricted to unstressed syllables; unclear whether the prominence was tonal or stress accent (p.3, 6-7, 8).
